guideTitle: The Best Curved Ultrawide Monitors, From VA to QD-OLED
metaTitle: Best Curved Ultrawide Monitors: 1500R vs 1800R, VA vs QD-OLED (2026)
metaDescription: We compared curved ultrawide monitors on curve radius, panel type, refresh rate, ports and warranty, from budget 34-inch VA panels to a 49-inch QD-OLED.
introParagraphs: A curve is described by its radius: 1500R means the screen follows a circle with a 1,500 mm radius, so a lower number is a tighter curve. Tighter curves wrap more at close range; gentler ones suit sitting further back and are often easier to live with for straight-edged work like spreadsheets and design.

Panel type matters as much as curve. VA panels offer strong contrast for the money, IPS-type panels tend to hold color better at an angle, and QD-OLED offers per-pixel contrast at a much higher price, with the burn-in caution that comes with OLED.

The seven monitors below run from about $205 to $900 at the time of writing: five 34-inch 1500R panels, a 34-inch 1800R QD-OLED and a 49-inch 1800R QD-OLED. Our comparison is based on published specifications, not hands-on testing.

sansui-34-curved.summary: A 34-inch 1500R VA panel at 200Hz with strong stated color, for the lowest price here.
sansui-34-curved.description:
The SANSUI is the lowest-cost way into a curved 3440 x 1440 ultrawide here, and its specification is strong for the price: a 1500R VA panel at 200Hz, with stated 97% DCI-P3 and 130% sRGB coverage and 3000:1 contrast.

It also supports HDR and picture-in-picture or picture-by-picture for two sources. For someone trying a curved ultrawide for the first time, it is the lowest-risk way to find out whether you like the format.

The listing doesn't state a warranty length, and there is no USB-C.
sansui-34-curved.bestFor: A first curved ultrawide for a desktop PC on a modest budget.
sansui-34-curved.skipIf: You want a stated warranty or USB-C; the ASUS TUF or Dell is the better fit.

asus-tuf-vg34vq3b-curved.summary: Four USB 3.2 ports, speakers and a three-year warranty on a 1500R VA panel.
asus-tuf-vg34vq3b-curved.description:
The ASUS TUF VG34VQ3B adds what the SANSUI lacks for a busy desk: four USB 3.2 ports, built-in speakers and a stated three-year warranty.

The panel is a 1500R VA at 180Hz with 90% DCI-P3. That is slightly less color coverage and a lower refresh rate than the SANSUI's figures, so the case for it is connectivity and warranty rather than picture.

There is no USB-C for laptop charging.
cons: Costs more than the SANSUI for similar core specs
Lower stated color coverage than the SANSUI
asus-tuf-vg34vq3b-curved.bestFor: A desktop setup with several USB peripherals where a stated warranty matters.
asus-tuf-vg34vq3b-curved.skipIf: You mainly want picture quality per dollar; the SANSUI covers that for less.

asus-tuf-fastips-curved.badge: Best for Color at an Angle
asus-tuf-fastips-curved.summary: An IPS-type 1500R panel at 250Hz, for steadier color than VA.
asus-tuf-fastips-curved.description:
The ASUS FastIPS model is the choice if you care about color consistency: IPS-type panels tend to shift color less than VA when viewed off-center, which helps with photo work and a wide screen whose edges you see at an angle.

It is also the fastest non-OLED panel here at 250Hz, with a stated 4000:1 contrast, 95% DCI-P3 and a three-year warranty.

It costs more than the VA models at similar sizes, and it has very little buyer feedback so far.
pros: Steadier color at an angle than VA
cons: Very little buyer feedback so far
Costs more than the VA models
asus-tuf-fastips-curved.bestFor: Photo and video work, or anyone who notices color shift at the edges of a wide screen.
asus-tuf-fastips-curved.skipIf: Deep blacks for movies and games matter more; a VA or QD-OLED panel is the better fit.

alienware-aw3425dwm-curved.summary: A 1500R VA panel with a console mode, a height-adjustable stand and a three-year warranty.
alienware-aw3425dwm-curved.description:
The Alienware AW3425DWM is the pick for a shared gaming setup: it is the only monitor here with a dedicated console mode.

Its 1500R VA panel runs at 180Hz with a stated 1ms response, 3000:1 contrast, 95% DCI-P3 and HDR400, and it adds a height-adjustable stand and a three-year warranty, which the SANSUI and ASUS VA models don't both offer.

It is still VA, so blacks won't match the QD-OLED models, and there is no USB-C.
alienware-aw3425dwm-curved.bestFor: A PC and console sharing one curved screen.
alienware-aw3425dwm-curved.skipIf: You only game on a PC and want the best value; the SANSUI covers that for less.

dell-34-plus-usbc-curved.summary: USB-C with 65W charging on a 1500R VA panel, with Dell's Premium Panel warranty.
dell-34-plus-usbc-curved.description:
The Dell 34 Plus is the one to choose if a laptop drives your desk: USB-C with 65W Power Delivery carries video and charging over a single cable.

Its 1500R VA panel runs at 120Hz with stated 99% sRGB and 95% DCI-P3, and Dell's Premium Panel warranty covers certain pixel defects. Dell lists a 0.03ms response time; brands measure response differently, so we wouldn't compare that figure directly with the others.

120Hz is the lowest refresh rate here, which is fine for office work but less suited to fast games.
cons: Costs more than the other 1500R VA models
dell-34-plus-usbc-curved.bestFor: A laptop-based home office that wants a curved ultrawide on one cable.
dell-34-plus-usbc-curved.skipIf: You play fast games on a desktop; the SANSUI or ASUS FastIPS is the better fit.

alienware-aw3425dw-qd-oled-curved.summary: A 34-inch 1800R QD-OLED at 240Hz with G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro.
alienware-aw3425dw-qd-oled-curved.description:
The AW3425DW is the step up to QD-OLED: per-pixel contrast (stated at 1,500,000:1), 240Hz, 99.3% DCI-P3 and HDR TrueBlack 400, with G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro and a three-year warranty.

Its 1800R curve is gentler than the 1500R VA models, which suits sitting a little further back or work where straight lines should look straight.

It costs more than twice as much as the VA models, and like any OLED, it carries a burn-in caution with static content such as taskbars; check the warranty terms.
specs: G-Sync + FreeSync Premium Pro; warranty: 3 years
cons: More than twice the price of the VA models
OLED burn-in caution with static content
Less wraparound than a 1500R curve at close range
alienware-aw3425dw-qd-oled-curved.bestFor: Gaming and media where contrast and motion matter, for buyers ready to spend more.
alienware-aw3425dw-qd-oled-curved.skipIf: Your screen shows static office content all day; a VA or IPS panel avoids OLED's burn-in caution.

samsung-odyssey-g93sc-49-curved.summary: A 49-inch 5120 x 1440 QD-OLED with an 1800R curve and picture-by-picture.
samsung-odyssey-g93sc-49-curved.description:
The Odyssey G93SC is the largest screen here, a 49-inch 5120 x 1440 QD-OLED, and the choice if you want the width of two monitors without a bezel down the middle.

It runs at 240Hz with stated 1,000,000:1 contrast and 99% DCI-P3, supports G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro, and picture-by-picture lets two sources share the width. The gentler 1800R curve suits the extra width better than a tight radius would.

It is the most expensive monitor here, it needs far more desk width and depth than a 34-inch screen, and it carries the same OLED burn-in caution as the AW3425DW.
pros: Width of two monitors without a bezel
cons: OLED burn-in caution with static content
samsung-odyssey-g93sc-49-curved.bestFor: A large desk where one screen replaces two, for gaming, trading or wide timelines.
samsung-odyssey-g93sc-49-curved.skipIf: Your desk is under about 55 inches wide or shallow; a 34-inch model is the better fit.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Match the curve to your distance and work
buyingCriteria.explanation: 1500R wraps more at close range and suits games and media; 1800R is gentler and suits sitting further back or straight-edged work. Larger screens generally pair with gentler curves.
VA gives strong contrast for the money; IPS-type panels tend to hold color better at an angle; QD-OLED gives per-pixel contrast but costs much more and carries a burn-in caution with static content.

A 34-inch ultrawide needs more width and depth than a standard monitor, and a 49-inch model needs considerably more. If you use a monitor arm, check it is rated for the monitor's weight without its stand and its VESA pattern.
USB-C with Power Delivery matters for a laptop; extra USB ports matter for a desktop full of peripherals. Here, only the Dell lists USB-C charging.

faq.a: It is the radius of the curve in millimeters. A lower number is a tighter curve: 1500R wraps more than 1800R.

faq.q: Is a tighter curve always better?
faq.a: No. Tighter curves feel more immersive at close range; gentler curves can be easier for straight-edged work and suit larger screens. Choose by use and distance.

faq.q: Why does the 49-inch model use a gentler curve?
faq.a: Over a much wider screen, a tight curve would bend the far edges sharply. Larger ultrawides generally pair with gentler curves.
VA for contrast on a budget, IPS-type for steadier color at an angle, QD-OLED for the best contrast if you can accept the price and OLED's burn-in caution.

faq.q: Does a curved monitor need a special arm?
faq.a: It needs an arm rated for the monitor's weight without its stand and its VESA pattern. Heavier curved screens are worth pairing with an arm that leaves margin above that weight.

bottomLine: For most people trying a curved ultrawide, the SANSUI is the sensible start: a fast 1500R VA panel at the lowest price here. Choose the Dell if a laptop runs your desk, the Alienware AW3425DWM for a PC-and-console setup, or the ASUS FastIPS if color consistency matters.

If you're ready to spend more, the Alienware AW3425DW brings QD-OLED contrast to a 34-inch screen, and the Samsung Odyssey G93SC replaces two monitors with one 49-inch panel, provided your desk has room.
